text: Masters, treat your slaves justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
Devote yourselves to prayer, staying alert in it with thanksgiving.
Pray for us as well, that God may open a door for the word, so that we may declare the mystery of Christ—for which I am in chains—
and that I may make it plain, as I ought to speak.

versions.text: and that I may make it known as clearly as I ought to speak it.
versions.explanation: The Greek φανερώσω means 'reveal/make clear'; 'make it known as clearly' is slightly redundant and the doubled 'it' at the end makes the line clumsy for oral reading. A tighter rendering reads more naturally aloud while keeping the sense of obligation in δεῖ με λαλῆσαι.

versions.text: and that I may make it clear, as I ought to speak.
versions.explanation: The sense of φανερώσω (make manifest/plain) is preserved, but the comma-break before an object-less "as I ought to speak" leaves the line hanging when read aloud. "Make it plain" pairs more naturally with the following clause and keeps the obligation of δεῖ με λαλῆσαι intact. Nothing is missing from the Greek in the current reading — αὐτὸ is represented by "it" — so this is a rhythm improvement only.

text: Conduct yourselves wisely toward outsiders, making the most of every opportunity.
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how to answer each person.
Tychicus will tell you all about my situation. He is a beloved brother, a faithful servant and fellow slave in the Lord.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts.
With him comes Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.
Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and so does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, about whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, welcome him.
Jesus, who is called Justus, also greets you. These are the only ones from among the circumcised who are my coworkers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ, greets you. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, that you may stand mature and fully convinced in everything God wills.
For I testify that he works hard for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.

versions.text: For I testify that he works hard for you and for those in Laodicea and Hierapolis.
versions.explanation: The Greek repeats τῶν ἐν before both cities, distinguishing the two communities. Repeating 'those in' preserves the parallel structure and gives the sentence a better cadence when read aloud.

text: Luke, our beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.
Give my greetings to the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church that meets in her house.
After this letter has been read to you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.
And tell Archippus: "See to the ministry you have received in the Lord, and complete it."
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
